summary.text: The proof handles values below the thresholds by exhaustive trial-division searches, while above them positivity directly gives \(n=p+q\) for even \(n\) and \(n=p+2q\) for odd \(n\). For any bound \(a\), applying positivity to \(N=2a+8014\) yields primes \(p-6,p\) with \(p>q\), which forces \(p-6>a\) and hence gives arbitrarily large cousin-prime pairs.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 c(n)=1+(n\bmod 2).
\]
Thus \(c(n)=1\) when \(n\) is even and \(c(n)=2\) when \(n\) is odd. For a given \(q\), put
\[
 p=n-c(n)q.
\]
The sequence value \(A219055(n)\) counts those \(q<n\) for which
\[
 (c(n)+1)q<n,
\]
\(q\), \(q+6\), \(p\), and \(p-6\) are all prime. The displayed inequality guarantees in particular that subtraction in the definition of \(p\) is genuine and that
\[
 p=n-c(n)q>q.
\]
Consequently these are precisely representations of the required form
\[
 n=p+c(n)q=p+q\frac{3-(-1)^n}{2}
\]
with \(p>q\) and with \(p,q,p-6,q+6\) prime.

Assume the core conjecture:

* if \(n>8012\) is even, then \(A219055(n)>0\);
* if \(n>15727\) is odd, then \(A219055(n)>0\).

We prove the three asserted conclusions.

First, we record the finite facts needed below the two thresholds. They are established by exhaustive trial division and exhaustive search. For completeness, here is the exact mathematical content and justification of those computations.

For an integer \(N\), primality was tested as follows. First require \(N\ge 2\). The number \(2\) is accepted. Every other accepted number is required to be odd. Starting with \(d=3\), test the successive odd integers
\[
 3,5,7,\ldots
\]
as long as \(d^2\le N\). If one of them divides \(N\), reject \(N\); if the first \(d\) with \(d^2>N\) is reached without finding a divisor, accept \(N\). The implementation gives this process \(N\) recursive steps, which is more than enough for every successful run relevant here; moreover, running out of steps causes rejection, so it can never produce a false assertion of primality.

To see directly that every accepted number is prime, suppose that an odd \(N\ge2\) has been accepted. If it were composite, it would have a divisor \(m\) satisfying
\[
 2\le m\le \sqrt N.
\]
If \(m\) were even, then \(2\mid N\), contrary to the oddness of \(N\). If \(m\) were odd, then \(m\ge3\), \(m^2\le N\), and the trial division would have tested \(m\) and rejected \(N\). Thus no such divisor exists, and \(N\) is prime. Equivalently, the recursive soundness argument is this: after the test has passed the odd candidate \(d\), no odd divisor \(m\ge d\) with \(m^2\le N\) exists. If the procedure stops because \(N<d^2\), this is immediate; otherwise \(d\nmid N\), and every larger odd \(m\) is at least \(d+2\), so the assertion follows from the remaining recursive tests.

For Goldbach representations of an integer \(n\), the finite search examines every \(q=0,1,\ldots,n-1\), and declares success if
\[
 q\le n,\qquad q\text{ is prime},\qquad n-q\text{ is prime}.
\]
Every successful search therefore supplies primes \(q\) and \(p=n-q\), and the bound \(q\le n\) ensures
\[
 n=(n-q)+q=p+q.
\]
For Lemoine representations, the search likewise examines every \(q=0,1,\ldots,n-1\), and declares success if
\[
 2q\le n,\qquad q\text{ is prime},\qquad n-2q\text{ is prime}.
\]
Every success therefore supplies primes \(q\) and \(p=n-2q\) satisfying
\[
 n=p+2q.
\]

Direct exhaustive evaluation of these searches, using the sound primality test just described, gives the following two finite facts:

1. For every \(n<8013\), at least one of the following holds: \(n<4\), \(n\) is odd, or the Goldbach search succeeds for \(n\).
2. For every \(n<15728\), at least one of the following holds: \(n<7\), \(n\) is even, or the Lemoine search succeeds for \(n\).

These statements amount respectively to checking the finite lists \(0,1,\ldots,8012\) and \(0,1,\ldots,15727\). The irrelevant entries are discharged by the first two alternatives, while each relevant entry is supplied with an explicitly found pair of primes by the corresponding search. By the soundness argument above, the reported factors really are prime. It follows that:

* every even \(n\) with \(4\le n\le8012\) is a sum of two primes;
* every odd \(n\) with \(7\le n\le15727\) is of the form \(p+2q\) with \(p,q\) prime.

We now prove Goldbach's conjecture. Let \(n\ge4\) be even. If \(n\le8012\), the first finite fact supplies primes \(p,q\) with \(n=p+q\). Suppose instead that \(n>8012\). The core conjecture gives \(A219055(n)>0\), so at least one term is counted. Hence there is a \(q\) such that
\[
 (c(n)+1)q<n,
\]
with \(q\), \(q+6\), \(n-c(n)q\), and \(n-c(n)q-6\) prime. Since \(n\) is even, \(n\bmod2=0\), so \(c(n)=1\). Thus
\[
 2q<n
\]
and both \(q\) and \(n-q\) are prime. Taking
\[
 p=n-q
\]
gives
\[
 n=p+q.
\]
This handles every even \(n\ge4\), proving Goldbach's conjecture.

Next we prove Lemoine's conjecture. Let \(n\ge7\) be odd. If \(n\le15727\), the second finite fact supplies primes \(p,q\) with \(n=p+2q\). Suppose instead that \(n>15727\). Again \(A219055(n)>0\), so there is a counted \(q\) satisfying the conditions above. Since \(n\) is odd, \(n\bmod2=1\), and therefore \(c(n)=2\). In particular,
\[
 3q<n,
\]
and both \(q\) and \(n-2q\) are prime. Taking
\[
 p=n-2q
\]
gives
\[
 n=p+2q.
\]
Thus every odd \(n\ge7\) has a Lemoine representation, proving Lemoine's conjecture.

It remains to prove that there are infinitely many primes \(r\) for which \(r+6\) is also prime. We prove the stronger unboundedness statement that for every nonnegative integer \(a\), there is such an \(r>a\).

Fix \(a\), and set
\[
 N=2a+8014.
\]
This number is even and satisfies \(N>8012\). By the core conjecture, \(A219055(N)>0\). Choose a counted \(q\). Since \(N\) is even, \(c(N)=1\), and the defining conditions give
\[
 2q<N,
\]
together with the primality of
\[
 q,\quad q+6,\quad N-q,\quad N-q-6.
\]
Set
\[
 r=N-q-6.
\]
Then \(r\) is prime. Also \(N-q-6\) being prime implies that it is at least \(2\); in particular \(N-q\ge8\), so the subtraction is not truncated and
\[
 r+6=N-q.
\]
The latter number is prime as well. Hence \((r,r+6)\) is a cousin-prime pair.

We must show that this pair lies beyond the prescribed bound \(a\). From
\[
 2q<N=2a+8014
\]
and integrality, we obtain
\[
 q\le a+4006.
\]
Therefore
\[
 r=2a+8014-q-6
  \ge 2a+8014-(a+4006)-6
  =a+4002>a.
\]
Thus for every \(a\) there exists an \(r>a\) such that both \(r\) and \(r+6\) are prime.

Finally, any subset of the nonnegative integers that contains an element larger than every prescribed bound is infinite: a finite set has a largest element, which would itself be a bound for all its elements. Applying this observation to
\[
 \{r\in\mathbb N:r\text{ is prime and }r+6\text{ is prime}\}
\]
shows that this set is infinite.

We have therefore deduced from the core positivity conjecture all three conclusions: Goldbach's conjecture, Lemoine's conjecture, and the infinitude of cousin-prime pairs \((p,p+6)\).
